input:
In this example, we will examine the performance of a vapour-compression refrigeration unit serving a cold store, evaporating at 0 °C and condensing at 45 °C. The coefficient of performance, which is essentially the refrigeration effect divided by the work input, provides a convenient measure of how effectively the unit converts work into cooling. Between the two temperatures in question, the Carnot coefficient of performance is 6.07, and this value represents the theoretical maximum that no real cycle operating between 0 °C and 45 °C can exceed, regardless of how carefully it is designed or operated.

The installed unit, however, achieves a coefficient of performance of only 2.44, which is considerably lower than the Carnot value of 6.07. This gap arises because the ideal cycle does not account for a range of real-world losses, including pressure drops in the lines and heat exchangers, irreversibilities within the compressor, and heat transfer taking place across finite temperature differences in both the evaporator and the condenser. It is important to note that none of these individual contributions is separated out in the manufacturer's figure, which is simply a single overall test value for the complete unit.

Furthermore, the manufacturer's test was carried out at full load, so the stated value of 2.44 strictly applies to that particular operating condition. Part-load performance is not stated, and this is a significant limitation, because a cold store does not necessarily call for full load at all times. At part load, the balance between fixed losses and useful refrigeration shifts, and the coefficient of performance will move accordingly, in a direction that the available figure does not allow us to determine. Consequently, any seasonal energy estimate based on 2.44 will inevitably carry an unquantified degree of error, and the figure of 2.44 is really best suited to comparing units that have been tested in the same way, rather than to predicting actual running costs with any confidence. Any use of 2.44 outside the full-load condition should therefore be treated as provisional.
target:
A vapour-compression unit serving a cold store evaporates at 0 °C and condenses at 45 °C, and its coefficient of performance at full load is 2.44 against a Carnot value of 6.07 between the same temperatures. The coefficient of performance is the refrigeration effect divided by the work input. The Carnot value is the highest the ratio can reach for a cycle working between the two temperatures: it is fixed by the temperatures alone, and no machine exceeds it.

The gap between 2.44 and 6.07 is the sum of the losses the ideal cycle omits: pressure drops in the lines and exchangers, irreversibility in the compressor, and heat transfer across finite temperature differences in the evaporator and the condenser. None of these losses is separated in the manufacturer's figure, which is a single test value for the whole unit, and the split between them cannot be recovered from it.

The two temperatures set the limit through the lift the cycle must provide. Heat is taken up at 0 °C and rejected at 45 °C, and every loss inside the machine is paid for across that lift; a wider lift at the same refrigeration duty would lower the Carnot value itself and lower the achieved value with it. The achieved 2.44 is therefore a property of the unit at its stated temperatures, not a rating that transfers to a warmer condenser or a colder evaporator.

The manufacturer's test was run at full load, and the stated 2.44 belongs to that condition. Part-load performance is not stated, and the cold store does not call for full load at all times: at part load the balance between fixed losses and useful refrigeration shifts, and the coefficient of performance moves with it, in a direction the available figure does not fix. A seasonal energy estimate built on 2.44 carries an unquantified error, and the figure supports comparison between units tested the same way rather than a prediction of running cost.
